utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I Your Honour, I wonder if - it would be very brief - if we could go into private session for me to raise a point related to protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Stewart [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, immediately before the adjourned yesterday evening, we were considering a meeting which you had with Mr. Izetbegovic in early April, 1992. And the next question is, Mr. Krajisnik, what was the content of the discussion between you and Mr. Izetbegovic at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject of our discussion was actually the solution we were looking for in order to stop the war, and one of the main analytical issues we discussed was the issue of Sarajevo, because the war started in Sarajevo, and we thought it was the most difficult territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if it is possible to say that's the way the discussion went, did proposals come primarily from you or primarily from Mr. Izetbegovic or was it evenly to'ing and fro'ing of suggestions on how to resolve the situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the first issue, that's how to stop the war, we talked spontaneously. It was an exchange based on our mutual desire to find a way to stop the armed conflict, because we both realised that it had already reached serious dimensions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a -- a nub of the potential solutions under discussion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the entire conflict culminated in Sarajevo -- maybe I didn't explain the background well enough, but if you want to hear it, I can explain what this peace rally was all about. It took place in Sarajevo, and before that, in the negotiations, we presented maps, and it was suggested that the entire Bosnia be transformed into three constituent units, whereas Sarajevo, according to one proposal, should have been under the government of the United Nations for a while pending a solution. Since the war started in Sarajevo and both of us were natives of Sarajevo, I told him, "Let's find a temporary solution for Sarajevo just to stop the war and then continue looking for a final solution during peace." And as Mr. Kecmanovic testified, we talked in fact exactly as Mr. Kecmanovic described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have one small correction to make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We heard you say you have one small correction to make, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correction I have to make is in fact to the description given by Mr. Kecmanovic. The two of us agreed that he should propose a solution. He sent his proposal to Pale, and according to him he didn't receive a reply from the leadership. I did not receive that proposal he sent, because at the time I was in Zabrdje at the other end of town, and I don't know any details about what he sent and how and to whom. For a while, he wasn't aware of it, but I was in Zabrdje, not at Pale. Mr. Koljevic was there, however, and he replied, probably after consultations with others, and his answer was positive, affirmative. But I didn't answer, didn't respond to his proposal because I hadn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you deal with these questions to a considerable extent by saying, well, it was exactly as Mr. Kecmanovic described. These proposals were not explored in any great detail in the course of Mr. Kecmanovic's evidence. Is it correct you -- it was you rather than Mr. Kecmanovic who was the -- the source of proposed solutions on the Serb side, wasn't it, at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, in order to assist the cessation of hostilities, I told Mr. Izetbegovic it would be a good idea to find a temporary solution for Sarajevo. That was later qualified by some people as a suggestion to divide Sarajevo, and that is very far from the truth. Mr. Izetbegovic said, "Well, suggest something." And I replied, "It would be best if we sat down together to discuss it based on ethnic areas. Let us find that solution on a temporary basis just to stop the war." And then he said, "Let's have Mr. Kecmanovic prepare that temporary solution." Mr. Kecmanovic seemed a bit reluctant but finally accepted. However, I didn't have any contacts with either him or Mr. Izetbegovic after that. I have in fact another correction. When Mr. Kecmanovic said that I had talked on the phone to Mr. Izetbegovic about the issue of Sarajevo, that that conversation was not about Sarajevo. I called him up because my trip from Zabrdje to Ilidza was marked by an incident. A Muslim police car stopped us on the road, and they captured my escorts. So from Ilidza I called up late Izetbegovic and asked him to have those people released. He told me he wasn't aware of that incident, but at the end of the day he had them released. That was the reason why I called Izetbegovic, not to discuss Sarajevo. Maybe there was some misunderstanding between the two of them. But in any case, that telephone call had nothing to do with the meeting we had earlier in his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's return to the meeting, Mr. Krajisnik. What -- what essentially we heard from Mr. Kecmanovic was that to some extent Mr. Izetbegovic was saying to you, Mr. Krajisnik, come up with proposals, and you were saying to Mr. Izetbegovic come up with proposals, and at some point Mr. Kecmanovic prepared a number of alternative proposals which he then sent to Pale. But perhaps to remind you, Mr. Krajisnik, what was not explored in Mr. Kecmanovic's evidence is the content of those proposals, what the suggested solutions were for Sarajevo. So my invitation, a question, in other words, to you, Mr. Krajisnik, is to explain. And it may have to be fairly full explanation. Explain to the Trial Chamber, Mr. Krajisnik, what the situation was in Sarajevo and what the possible solutions were for the temporary separation or temporary division of Sarajevo that you have mentioned. You've -- we brought up the map of Sarajevo from the vault, the P284, in case that is of any assistance to you. We also, of course, still have the map from yesterday, which is at page 25 of the map book, 5 -- P527, in case that should help as well, because it does occur to me that map is likely to be of some assistance in offering such an explanation. It might be the map needs to be different and physically placed for you to be able to use it, Mr. Krajisnik. Perhaps while this is happening, Mr. Krajisnik, it might be a useful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, is it -- I do understand it's not very comfortable, but is it still workable for the interpreters? Yes, it seems to be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I was only going to offer a gentle reminder but you probably -- and I don't suppose this is in dispute, you probably know more about Sarajevo than everybody else in this the courtroom at the moment will do, put together, for the rest of our lives and please bear that in mind with your explanations. We've picked up plenty in the course of the case but there is that fairly big gap still. So take it at the appropriate speed, Mr. Krajisnik, is what I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see here is the urban part of Sarajevo. This, roughly, is downtown. Old town municipality, in other words. This, roughly, is Novo Sarajevo municipality. This is municipality Novi Grad. This is Ilidza municipality, and this is Vogosca municipality. You see, Your Honours, that there are urban parts here, on one hand, and outskirts covered by villages. Do you see how the population is concentrated? In this area here, we have the largest concentration of -- largest density of population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know how it works. I wonder if it's possible I don't know if the camera -- I don't know whether it does it automatically, I wonder if it's possible for the video camera to stay on the map because otherwise the transcript later will be hard to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent it is permitted under the directive for the technicians, because there are certain instructions so as to put a Judge on the screen who speaks, which is done now, as you may see. To the extent compatible with that, and especially when Mr. Krajisnik is pointing at the map that we should focus as much as possible on the map. Let's proceed, and I'll keep an eye on it that we don't have to explain for the record that -- to say in words what Mr. Krajisnik is doing on the map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I had in mind. Thank you. I hope Your Honour's direction overrides that directive for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, as long as we are speaking, I take it that Mr. Krajisnik will not continue to point at the map with the pointer but you see that usually the one who speaks is on the screen. It's part of the directive. Let's see if we can also follow on our screens the explanation of Mr. Krajisnik. If there would be a very specific issue because this is just generally pointing at the areas of Sarajevo but if it comes to some detail it might be necessary to repeat something and to point at some movements in words as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you see, municipalities are divided this way. Along this edge, if I can put it that way, of this urban area we had the so-called blockade siege of Sarajevo. And I say so-called. I'll explain why. These are Serbian neighbourhoods, and everybody took up positions in their own neighbourhood. Above, overlooking this urban area, is Pale, towards the east. Towards the south is Trnovo. You can't see it now. Behind Vogosca, as you go further north, is Ilijas. Behind Ilidza is Hadzici municipality. Those are satellite municipalities that later became integral parts of the town of Sarajevo. At the point when things culminated and armed conflict began, all of this remained in Muslim hands. So if we're talking about the town, the town is in Muslim hands. However, in their ethnic areas, the Serbs had their ethnic areas covering meadows, forests, et cetera. We had the largest concentration of Serbs here, maybe 100.000, and another 30.000 on the periphery. So we talked. If anybody should want to divide Sarajevo for economic purposes, leaving everybody where they were, it was necessarily always to the disadvantage of the Serbian side because there were Serbs on both sides. So the proposal was as follows: This is the centre, the downtown area. Serbs held some villages here and here. And this largest area, the urban area, was held by Muslims. And the proposal at the time was to freeze things as they were pending a fair solution for transforming Sarajevo that we would continue to look for. You see, this concentration of the population here is ten times larger than the entire population of the periphery. So they have 80 per cent, the Serbs of the territory, and 10 per cent in town, in the Muslim area. This is Zabrdje, which I called the historic place. So from here I went to Ilidza, and Mr. Karadzic came from Pale. You see this airfield here, in an armoured vehicle, in fact a combat vehicle, the army drove him there to Ilidza. So if you had a situation like that leaving everybody where they were in their neighbourhoods, there was a basis for this temporary solution. When we talked to Cutileiro on the 18th or the 19th of March, you can read exactly in the newspaper what Karadzic said about how we needed to transform the town. There should have been ex-territorial areas state authorities buildings divided among the sites, et cetera, but that was not the subject of our conversation. The subject of our discussions was to find a temporary solution to stop the war and to continue talking, to have the conference going on. Without a map it's very difficult to understand Sarajevo. When you see this large blue blob, it doesn't mean anything. And this territory here, it turns out that a whole blue area is very large belonging to Serbs, whereas there are only 10.000 there, whereas in this smaller urban area there were 3 or 400.000 people. You see locations here, like Hrasnica. This too. This is also Hrasnica. The airport was between -- in the line of fire, and you couldn't cross to the other side without running into trouble. You heard witnesses talking about that. Not even theoretically were I able to go to Lukavica, whereas Karadzic and Koljevic were able to cross because they were driven in a combat vehicle, and they went to Ilidza to meet Mr. Cutileiro, whereas I was going from Zabrdje, and this is how -- this is where they captured our military patrol about which I called up Mr. Izetbegovic, asking him to intervene. All these areas here were separate towns into -- at one point but eventually incorporated into Sarajevo and turned into real towns. They became satellite neighbourhoods, municipalities. They were still, however, 30 or 40 kilometres away from the centre of the town. This picture is very telling. One witness talked about dividing municipalities. Do you know how the borders of municipalities run? They run zigzag like streets. The border of one municipality is a street, and the same is true of another. You have to write down the names of streets, and that's the way to divide municipalities. Sometimes the same street runs through two municipalities. The solution for Bosnia was not supposed to apply to Sarajevo as well. Sarajevo needed its own particular solution for -- for its purposes. That is why it looks on all maps, and it is in fact true, that Serbs are around this central area, whereas most of the Muslims are within that centre. And that was doable within 24 hours. Everybody would simply standstill in their ethnic area. You can see that on the map where the municipalities are divided, too. It's exactly this way the urban area that I referred to, outside an area that belongs to a municipality as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- the various different ways of producing a temporary solution that were under discussion at the meeting, were they variations on a theme in the sense that they were relatively modest differences from a basically -- from basically the same essential plan, or were they radically different possibilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who actually carried out the urban organisation of Sarajevo intentionally included the Serb and Muslim parts. It was the Muslims who were a majority in almost the entire area. This wasn't actually intentional. Whoever did it did not just take the central part and divide that off. Now, if you look at this here, when Witness Krsman Sinisa talked about this, he talked about Zabrdje, for 300 years that village was there, and authorities were based here in Novi Grad, and you couldn't even get a permit to build a house. Our proposal was to transform Sarajevo to have several municipalities in order to resolve local matters at local level. Now, Mr. Stewart is asking whether there were any major differences involved. It suited the Muslim side not to touch this kind of organisation, because they had a majority in practically every municipality except for one municipality maybe, especially when national parties came to power. If you recall the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, they legalised everything, all the houses that had been built illegally, buildings that were supposed to be torn down, people who moved in and illegally built houses and changed the ethnic pattern over the past ten years. Everybody knows that in Sarajevo. It's a different thing, the fact that in socialism you weren't allowed to talk about things like that without being called a nationalist, a chauvinist, or whatever. But there were two proposals. They didn't want anything to be changed. Before, when the talks were held with Mr. Cutileiro and in their map, Your Honours, you will see that Sarajevo completely belonged to the federation, whereas in our map, in the Serb map, and in Cutileiro's map, it was supposed to be under the UN for the time being and then to work for a transformation that would be satisfactory to all. It was impossible to divide Sarajevo. That is not true that I wanted some kind of walls to be built or whatever. We should simply have a larger number of municipalities so that people could have freedom at local level to resolve issues related to waterworks, electricity, and what have you not. So when I talked to Mr. Izetbegovic, I felt Mr. Izetbegovic's wish to have this stopped. At least that's the impression I had. And he -- that's why he said, "Well, Mr. Kecmanovic, why don't you work out for a proposal and let's discuss it then. It's better to discuss this than to wage a war." I have to tell the truth. That's the impression I got. I did not get an answer. I did not see Mr. Kecmanovic's proposal because he seen that to Pale, and I was in Zabrdje at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the -- do you know this, then, Mr. Krajisnik: The proposals that Mr. Kecmanovic was to produce, did they essentially amount to a drawing of boundaries for the purposes of this proposed temporary division?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No boundaries. We have several minutes there and records where we always took Geneva as an example. There is one town around Geneva. I know. I was there. It's a French town, I think. I think -- I cannot remember its name now. So this was this restaurant that was half in France and half in Switzerland. The only thing we wanted was to have a transformation of a big city, and Brussels was an example where somebody would have a particular neighbourhood where they could resolve problems related to utilities, for example. Your Honours, may I just remind you that during the First World War Rajlovac was better known than Sarajevo, and people were saying where is this Sarajevo? Is it near Rajlovac? However, Rajlovac remained a backwater because everything was done in Sarajevo. Economic questions were important. Universities were there too. And why would we not have hospitals, schools, universities, stadiums? Everybody should use that. We cannot build new ones for ourselves, so let's just regulate life according to our needs, and that's what we wanted to do. You saw the municipality of Novi Grad. They wouldn't let Rajlovac have a local commune. They didn't allow the procedure to be initiated. It was simply out-voted. Mr. Kecmanovic never would have proposed any boundaries or any divisions. These would be "boundaries" of municipalities. He went a bit beyond that. He said, "Well, would this do in terms of transforming Sarajevo?", as far as I understood him then. And he also wrote something in newspaper articles, that he gave some solutions that could some day be a basis for a final solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it occurs to me that -- that the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it occurs to me that -- that the word I used in English, "boundaries," may be tendentious as you're hearing it in a way that I hadn't intended. The -- were the -- the variations of the proposals, they involved drawing different lines on the map for the purposes of the temporary division, did they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, boundaries, divisions, these are sensitive words. If I were speaking freely, I would speak freely and use those words, that there are municipalities and there are boundaries between municipalities in a city but the town was not divided. There are no boundaries between municipalities. It's not that you see something that is a border like an interstate border. There is a demarcation line, what municipality a particular neighbourhood belongs to. So from that point of view you're right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the temporary -- you used the word "standstill," Mr. Krajisnik. What did you have in mind? Would a standstill involve -- well, what degree of restrictions, if any, on the movement of people between one part of the city and another?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what we didn't want. First of all, that is impossible. If everybody is satisfied in the city of Sarajevo throughout the territory, if everybody stayed where they were, there are no boundaries. There is normal communication. Communication is normal now, too, except that people are not where they were. I mean, Serbs are not where they were before. But the point was that now you should have certain autonomy in decision-making in an area that you're interested in. And of course -- well, there's a proposal here, a proposal in terms of what we wanted exactly. That proposal was in New York -- or, rather, in Dayton, that the city would have a government of its own, that there would be several municipalities, that there would be a proper transformation. We always wanted the entire city of Sarajevo to have its own government, because there are many things that are common things. There is a tram that goes through four municipalities. There is a bus that goes through four municipalities. It would be insane if somebody wanted to do all of that separately. For an individual citizen, the municipality is the government. That's where you get a permit to build a house. That's where you regulate waterworks, electricity, and so on, and that is what people were lacking and that's what they said. Why did they have to go to the centre for all of this? Can something not be built here where we are? That's what Mr. Krsman told you. Here's Zabrdje, right here. It is more beautiful than Paris, Madrid, or The Hague, and they wanted to make a dump there, and indeed this is where they built the city dump. I was in the socialist alliance of working people and they wanted to build a cemetery there and I did my best to prevent moving that cemetery there. And why? Because they are reaching decisions at the level of the entire city and they don't care about our neighbourhood. They later moved it ten kilometres away into a wasteland where there is no one anyway, but first they wanted to build it there. When my house was discussed, for example, the Krajisnik family was there for 300 years. My house was built as a temporary house. I couldn't even build a -- I couldn't even get a credit. And it was only with this Mr. Hadzic I started this procedure for legalising it. And on the other side there were these big neighbourhoods that were being built without any permits at all. I'm not -- I don't want to offend any ethnic group, but you have lived there since time immemorial and they don't care about you. They want to build a city dump there. They want to have a cemetery there, and so on and so forth. That's why they were saying I was the greatest protector of Sarajevo. Let anybody show me any proposal where I said that I wanted a division of Sarajevo. This is all wrong. It was supposed to be a single city. What was suggested was not good. This Rajlovac after the Second World War was a municipality. It was a thriving municipality at the time, and then it was abolished, and then it was nothing. I'm sorry, I think I'm being very emotional when I'm saying all of this. Of course I know what Zabrdje is and what these other three cities are, on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to try to get to the -- the heart of what was involved in a practical sense in this temporary division. And the way I invite you to explain it is this: If the temporary division of Sarajevo came about in the ways that you were discussing with Mr. Izetbegovic, what would have been the essential differences between the way that people then lived and worked and the city went about its business under that temporary division as compared with the way it had all happened before this conflict even broke out?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in one municipality, and I worked in another municipality, and that's the way it would have been even after that. But I would resolve all the issues I care about in my own neighbourhood, in my own municipality. I would not allow the city dump to be there. I would perhaps have a different kind of factory there. I went to university right here in the centre of Sarajevo. This is where my university was. Every day I took the train or bus and went there. I love that city. And after all, if you want to be a civilised man, you cannot meet all your needs in a village. You need a theatre. You need a football stadium. All of that was in the urban area, and all of that was in Muslim hands at the time. And after all -- well, it doesn't matter. There are some Serbs there too. And quite simply that would not have been a problem. The problem was that all the surrounding neighbourhoods were discriminated against, on the outskirts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the temporary division that was under discussion, Mr. Krajisnik, was it contemplated that there would be any sort of checkpoints, anybody manning or monitoring any lines between different areas of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our objective was to eliminate precisely that kind of thing, quite simply to say, See, we've reached an agreement. Now you know where the municipality boundaries are, the temporary boundaries or whatever. So simply to bring the war to an end in that way. It was only in wartime that there were these checkpoints and some kind of armed units. But in the future, I think that there is no town where there are checkpoints between municipalities. I was in Geneva, and over there I saw that even though there are two different states there, there is nothing very formal about it. Even half of the airport is in Switzerland and the other half in France, and nobody's bothered by that. I'm sorry that I'm talking about all of these things now. I repeat, we accepted Bosnia-Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state with a seat in the UN. There can be no internal boundaries. How can we divide Sarajevo if Bosnia is not being divided, if this is a single international subject with its own internationally recognised borders?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, bearing in mind that Geneva hasn't for a very long time as far as I'm aware emerged from a violent civil conflict, so that -- that analogy to some extent might be put on one side. In the immediate future, if you did reach a temporary division by way of solution [sic], did you have in mind that Sarajevo could return more or less immediately to the same way of life that it had enjoyed before any of this conflict emerged?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right. The only unresolved question in this map was Sarajevo. Look at the Cutileiro map. And that is why I proposed the following: Let us work out a temporary solution, and then let's sit down and bring this conference to an end slowly but steadily. I saw that there was a lack of goodwill, and the Cutileiro Plan was given up on. Perhaps it was this group around Mr. Izetbegovic that influenced him to reject this proposal that had initially been adopted, the proposal made by Mr. Kecmanovic. I don't know how Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic reacted at the time, but nothing would have changed. We have would have just had peace. I'm confident of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss at the meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic the -- the conflict in the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps by way of introduction we said that everything should be done in order to have peace. The meeting was not a very long one, so it's not that we could discuss Derventa and, I don't know, other towns, apart from that subject that we were discussing. I'm not sure that we didn't even mention anything else. I don't know. I don't think we discussed anything broader. The curfew was almost there, so I had to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, and I mean you singular, Mr. Krajisnik, for the purpose of this question, did you consider that if there could be a temporary solution to stop the fighting in Sarajevo that there would also be rapidly an end to the conflict in the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did not think that, I would not have risked going into Sarajevo where I could have been killed, where there was shooting. I was deeply convinced that if we met up and if we found a solution it paid off to run the risk of going into Sarajevo. There was shooting there, and you're just taking a car and going into town. I was fully confident. I said I was going there, and I believe that things would be worked out, because after all, we all have families. It's a terrible thing when a war starts. Later on you sort of get used to it, but at the very outset you hope that you can somehow end it and you hope that it will be over any minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your awareness at the time of your meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic of the degree of violent conflict in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had very little information in Zabrdje in terms of what was going on elsewhere. There were so many problems in Sarajevo that perhaps I focused on that, receiving information about that, although I did not have sufficient information about that either. As for what was going on elsewhere, especially, for example, what a witness said here, he talked about what was going on in Zvornik, I absolutely did not attend that meeting. I didn't know about that. I'm saying by way of an illustration, now, whether he talked to somebody else or not I don't know, but I never saw, and I never attended that meeting, and I was not informed about what was going on elsewhere. Before the war I knew about the delegation that went to Bijeljina. I knew about the delegation that went to Kupres. I knew about the delegation that went to Brod. All of these delegations were delegations of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The only thing I knew is what I heard from them, but I could not exercise any influence in that regard and I didn't know anything about this in any detail. But during the war it was as if a curtain went down. People are bombarding you with misinformation, and it's so hard for you to tell what is true and what is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- did you get any ideas as to whether Mr. Izetbegovic was informed about the level of armed conflict, violent conflict in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say neither yes or no. We didn't talk about this as far as I can remember. It's not that he informed me. And I didn't really see any major changes regarding him. I mean, compared to what he was like before the conflict. We had a relaxed communication and perhaps even friendly. At any rate, it wasn't hostile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you, in the two weeks before this meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic, had you had any meeting or discussion with General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did attend one meeting with Mr. Kukanjac, and an intercept was played here. I don't remember in what capacity I attended that meeting, but I heard a lot of proposals, I remember, and Mr. Kukanjac rejected them all flat. Everybody was telling him, "You should go there now." Everybody thought the Yugoslav People's Army should come in and resolve all that. There were all sorts of proposals, but it wasn't - how shall I say? - a very serious topic. The talk was along the lines that the Yugoslav People's Army should side with the Serbs and defend them. But I remember Mr. Kukanjac said -- he's dead now, but I remember this. He said, "I'm here now, and as long as I live, I will treat all sides equally." He was completely neutral, and had he stayed on, that's how he would have acted. I did attend that one meeting. There was some local people there, local representatives. I can't remember everything they were saying, but in fact it was one intercept that I heard here that reminded me about this. None of those proposals came to pass eventually. But Mr. Kukanjac was a realistic man, and he didn't treat them very seriously. He, for his part, knew that they were wrong in thinking that the war was something less than serious and that everything can be dealt with easily as they thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, it appears that something hasn't come through in the translation. Mr. Sladojevic tells me there was a reference to a column of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your answer include some reference to what happened to a column of soldiers, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was talking about the neutrality of Mr. Kukanjac, I said that he treated all sides equally, Muslims and Serbs. And he would certainly have kept equal distance from both sides to the end if the Muslims hadn't attacked a column of his soldiers. But after that, they replaced him. I was saying that all the time he kept trying to find a solution and to remain neutral. He's dead now, but I'm talking the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Your Honour indicated that you wanted to take the break around this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said that if you would need to deal with certain matters that it was -- became urgent we would have an early --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, we're fairly near the break, Your Honour. Sometimes if we're trying to do a filing and that being 4.00, sometimes it's helpful to break a few minutes earlier and then we can get that done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break until ten minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the first thing I announce for the parties that there's a fair chance, I'm thinking in terms of close to 90 per cent, that tomorrow we'll have no third session in the afternoon but that we would finish at approximately 5.30. I can't say it for sure, but most likely we'll have a short day tomorrow. Then, Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With that heartbreaking news, Your Honour, I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, before the meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic and on that same day, you had had, from your evidence -- please say if this is wrong, you had had some meeting with the parties to the international negotiations the members of the European Community -- that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. But I've done a bit of reviewing. I'm not sure whether it was that meeting or not, but we had a meeting at Ilidza with Mr. Cutileiro. I think it was on that date, but it's still a long time ago. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then is it correct -- Mr. Krajisnik, if there's some doubt about these things in your recollection, then I'm quite sure the Trial Chamber would like to know those doubts. You had had a meeting with Mr. Tadic [sic] and Mr. Raguz, I think it was, and then you went home and returned, and then you met Mr. Izetbegovic, but did you have any other -- or Mr. Kecmanovic as well. Did you have any other meetings on at that day with completely other people than those that we've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction. It's Rasim Kadic and Martin Raguz. As for what you're asking me, I was at a meeting, I think, on the same date, certainly with Mr. Kadic and Raguz, but it was also attended by Mr. Kecmanovic and Mr. Pejanovic. It was that meeting at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- did you meet Mr. Prstojevic at any point on that day, with or without other people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I think, since it was at Ilidza, I believe we had some sort of meeting, but it didn't focus on the upcoming meeting. As I said, those people, Mr. Kecmanovic, Mr. Pejanovic, Mr. Kadic, Mr. Raguz, we met, but I don't remember any meeting that was attended by Mr. Prstojevic. I think he was there as a host.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, you think that Mr. Prstojevic was there but there as a host. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what would have been logical, because the leadership of Ilidza was there. They were present. They met us. They welcomed us when we came to Ilidza. I suppose he was there. I can't visualise anything any more. I can't remember the faces of that welcoming party. I suppose he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can't remember if you had any sort of, what I call broadly, a business meeting, a meeting at which you actually discussed with Mr. Prstojevic and other Ilidza representatives anything that was happening in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember another meeting on an another occasion, maybe a bit later, when we met with the leadership of Ilidza. That meeting was mentioned several times here in the courtroom with different views expressed about it. But as for that day when those people were there, I don't think we held a meeting with them, because I went home, then I returned, then I went to Sarajevo. I don't think I attended that meeting. I mean, that day when I was going to meet Mr. Izetbegovic. That's the day I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let -- let's concentrate, then, on what you referred to a moment ago as another meeting on another occasion, maybe a bit later when you said, "We met with the leadership of Ilidza." First of all, who is "we" who met with the Ilidza leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was in Zabrdje again. There was some ministers, then Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic. Maybe they even spent the night at Ilidza. Maybe they were staying for a while. They invited me, so I came to the meeting. And we had some sort of meeting without an agenda where everybody attended, the ministers, the leadership of Ilidza, maybe some other people too. That's the kind of meeting I mean. And the agenda was open-ended. We just discussed whatever came up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, if we can try to place it, Mr. Krajisnik. You've said you thought that it was after the -- "maybe a bit later" was your phrase. Maybe a bit later than the day of the meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic. Can you remember whether if this meeting with the Ilidza leadership was before or after you had moved to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, what's not what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was later relative to that meeting. I meant after that day, after the day of the meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic, maybe two or three days later. So it was not on the same day. It was maybe a couple of days later that we have -- that we had this meeting with the leadership of Ilidzas [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There must have been the -- the wrong words must have got picked up. There's been a mistranslation there, Mr. Krajisnik. I think I see how it may have happened. No, I wasn't saying -- I can see how it happened. I said maybe a bit later than the day. That might have been heard a bit later on the day. I wasn't suggesting it was the same day. I was simply picking up your answer that you said it was maybe a bit later than the Izetbegovic meeting, and I was therefore asking you if you were able to tell the Trial Chamber whether it was before or after you moved to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm really sorry. I only corrected it because I don't anything wrong to be picked up and to remain on the transcript. What I remember is this: I was at Pale on one day. I can explain for what reason. And then I returned to Zabrdje. I don't know how long after that I went to Pale again to remain, but from the records I've seen here, I know that I attended a session on the 15th of April, and on the 17th of April Mr. Karadzic wrote a letter whereby he withdrew all personnel. So I didn't resign on that day. I returned. When I went back again to Pale from Zabrdje, I don't know any more. I think quite a while later, maybe five, six, ten days later. Whatever I say now may turn out to be wrong. But to that meeting at Ilidza I came from Zabrdje. I was at Zabrdje at the time, not at Pale. As far as I remember. I'm really sorry. I am not precise, and I don't want anyone to -- to hold me to any one word I say, any one date. All I know is -- for certain is that I went to Pale -- I went from Zabrdje, not Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the meeting with the Ilidza leadership set up at their initiative or at the initiative of Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, you, or one of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't at my initiative, for sure. And second, as I said, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, and the ministers were there staying at Ilidza temporarily, and I got a message from them that I should come and talk to them. Since the hosts were there, we talked in their presence, and we mainly discussed subjects that were of interest to them. It was some sort of roundtable where everybody was free to take the floor, listen, ask questions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ministers you said who were staying at Ilidza temporarily, who were they? Which ministers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember all of them, but I know there was late Momcilo Pejic. I think Bozidar Antic was there. I'm not sure about anyone else, but there were more of them. I remember Pejic, very reasonable, down-to-earth man, an economist, a colleague of mine. I heard him speak. That's why I remember him being there. He was a minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was -- apart from Mr. Prstojevic, who was there as one of the representatives of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was Mr. Radoslav Unkovic, whose name we read in the papers we reviewed several times. There was MP Ljubo Bosiljcic, who is a native of that area, and I don't remember the others. I think Mr. Kezunovic was there. He was then president of the Executive Council or maybe the municipality. I don't know any more. I'm sure about the three -- the first three, whereas my memory about -- my memory of Mr. Kezunovic is a bit vague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic was in charge as far as the Ilidza group were concerned, was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was at the time. I think that he was the one who was in charge. Now, was he president of the or of the Crisis Staff, but he was - how should I put this? - he was the man at the top. The man who represented the Assembly of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you said that you mainly discussed subjects that were of interest to them. What were the subjects that were of interest to them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be quite honest. If I were to say everything I remembered, well, I remember very few things on my own. But having heard things here and having listened to the intercepts, I have a more complete picture. So I'm afraid I'm going to confuse the two a bit. However, the basic point is that the discussion focused on the situation as it was in Ilidza. There was a great deal of anxiety there. People wanted to know what these negotiations meant, these foreigners coming in and so on. This is a reference to international representatives. Also, what our position was with regard to some other matters, how far the negotiations have progressed. Is there a solution that we can hope for, and so on. Of course, there were all sorts of proposals, and people said things autonomously in discussions. It wasn't that there was a cohesive policy. Everybody spoke freely and said what they thought. Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic tried to present the international role and position as they were. So that was the problem. There was another problem too. One hundred metres away from the place where we were, were the separation lines between us and the Muslims, and there was a major attack that had been launched. A lot of people had lost their lives. So those were problems that were discussed too. I really cannot recall all details. I've been filling these voids in my memory, and that was the only thing I could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The major attack that had been launched, that was an attack by whom upon whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a major attack on Ilidza by the Muslim forces. I can not put this into a time frame, if I can put it that way. But what I know is that there was a representative of the European Community, Mr. Doyle, I think his name was, and then Mr. MacKenzie was there, and then Mrs. Plavsic had a role to play as well. Then they were getting the dead out as well. All of this happened in Ilidza. Now, when all of this happened, I cannot say. I'm afraid I'll make a mistake. The Muslims attacked from Hrasnica, right here. From that area. That's are the attack against Ilidza was launched. This is Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, a major attack. What was reported to you to indicate what was the size and severity of that attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the beginning of the war, it was quite terrible. As I said a few moments ago, when a war starts then even small things become big. Later on you get used to it. Quite simply, people organise themselves at their own initiative, and there was this small conflict with the representatives of the UN. They asked them to help them get the dead out and get the prisoners out. Chaos prevailed. Confusion prevailed. I heard all of that from a distance. Later on, I learned more things through different conversations, but this was an ugly baptism of fire if I can put it that way and things looked terrible at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps I should make it clear. It's precisely because of what you said in your last answer that when a war starts small things become big it's because of the nature of these things that I'm inviting you to become more specific. Was it from what you understood was it a dozen men, let's assume it was men, was it hundred -- I'm asking for some indication of what you understood at the time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we've digressed from your main question, the one that I gave an answer to. I talked about the meeting I attended and I said that there were different topics discussed. I do not remember all the topics. Then I mentioned that there was a war going on near the separation lines, and then I mentioned this unfortunate incident. Perhaps it occurred even after this meeting, because I do not recall the entire content. It was an open-ended agenda, as I said, but if you wanted me to talk about this incident without relating it to this meeting, then I'll try to explain everything I know to you. As far as I can remember, several Serbs were killed. Some were taken prisoner. Citizens were upset. None of us, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, or I, were there. Mrs. Plavsic was there from among the leadership because she was in Sarajevo. Then there were representatives of the UN too. That is to say UNPROFOR and the European Community. I know that Mr. Doyle was the representative and mediator. The other day on television I saw him and I heard him reminiscing about this, and that is how I remember more too. But speaking apart from this meeting, this incident was quite shocking. Quite simply, you now see what you only read about before. You see dead people. It's not a movie. It's not that there's red paint thrown around and then these people actually get up later. It was terrible for the area of Ilidza, and it was people from Hrasnica and Sokolovica Kolonija who attacked. It was these Muslim units from there that attacked Ilidza. Ilidza was in Serb hands. I mean the centre of Ilidza, although that's a smaller part of the municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I imagine it or did I hear you mention Hajat in the course of that answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I imagined it or you did?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my favourite TV station Hajat. They had an interview with Mr. Dole a few days ago, and he was reminiscing about this incident when he was there with Mrs. Plavsic trying to deal with this Muslim attack against Ilidza. That's the only TV station from Bosnia and Herzegovina that I can watch here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The main reason I mentioned it Your Honours, is it doesn't appear on the transcript so I wonder Mr. Krajisnik, again, possibly if you are going a little quickly if things are getting missed. Did the -- did the Ilidza leadership ask for any assistance, any help from you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to give a literal answer, there were no meetings held with representatives of any municipality without them having asked for help. They think that you're a magician who can solve all their problems. Especially here in Ilidza. People were frightened. And then it was a welcome opportunity for them when the leadership would come and then they would tell them about all their problems. Of course, since there was a war going on, they did not understand who was in charge of what. They are telling everybody everything. We need soldiers. We need this. We need that. All of this is quite normal in a war. First, you have to calm them down. You shouldn't refuse them. You should bear in mind their emotions, but you really have nothing that you can do in order to resolve their problems. Believe me, I was in that kind of situation hundreds of times. I didn't say, "That is not my line of work." I would try to listen and understand, and then the person talking to me would go away believing I was the right person to talk to. That's simply the way it was. Everybody from every municipality, when they felt threatened -- well, there are soldiers there and then there is information that there is a countless number of Muslims who are going to wipe them out, and so on and so forth. The situation was terrible. It was terrible listening to all of that. And you simply had no way of helping, no possibility of helping. You are talking to them in a political way. You are listening to what they have to say. You are making suggestions and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- the Muslim forces, you've said, Mr. Krajisnik, you don't know whether it was before or after this meeting, but when you did receive information about this Muslim attack against Ilidza, did you receive information about the identity of -- I don't mean the names of the individual men, but the identity of those Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be quite honest. I don't understand. For us, these were the Muslim armed forces. When I say that, I mean I didn't go into whether they were paramilitaries or not. It was the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats, and that was my understanding of it. In a war, all legal norms are forgotten. There is an armed Muslim, an armed Serb, an armed Croat. There were armed units, on the one hand and -- on one side and the other side. At that time, the Yugoslav People's Army was in existence, but -- how put I put this? This was a local conflict. We all call them the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, and so on and so forth, and that didn't have to be the case. Very soon they brought those units under the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So for us that was the Muslim side, the Muslim armed units and so on. I do not remember that we used any derogatory terms for them as they did for us, but at any rate it was Serbs, Croats, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met the Ilidza leadership, were you -- did you come away from that meeting with any clear picture as to the state of organisation of any armed forces on the Serb side in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were at that meeting with the leadership of Ilidza, most of what was going on was academic and theoretical debates. Everybody had proposals of different kinds. I didn't see a single soldier. They were probably out there at the line. What I heard from them is what my knowledge was. Perhaps I saw someone walking there, but they were at the line 100 metres away, but I did not see them. But we were that close. Well, what I remember is that individuals said they can't do anything to us, and that's what optimists were saying, but then pessimists said, no, they're wrong. It's people from Sandzak and there's three times more them. So you listen to different proposals and different contributions to the discussion. It's not that you can be an arbiter of any kind and you cannot get to the actual truth. The Serb side had some kind of Territorial Defence, and they said they would do everything they can to defend their own ethnic areas, which was the Serb area, yes. And on the other side were the areas where the Muslims were a majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- we don't need all to look at it, perhaps, but on the -- not your favourite map, but on P211, based on the 1991 census, Ilidza municipality as a whole is shown with a relative majority Muslims 43 per cent and Serbs 37 per cent. Is that consistent with your understanding of the position in Ilidza at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not consistent. Now I'm going to explain this to you. The municipality of Ilidza, as opposed to other municipalities -- well, the urban part of Ilidza was Serb, whereas this place, Hrasnica and Sokolovic, Kolonija, these are new neighbourhoods. There were a lot of buildings built without permits too. That is where Muslims moved in, especially from Sandzak. That is to say from Serbia and Montenegro, so a different region altogether. Now, there was a census in 1991, and it was never verified. And in 1990, the elections were held, and all citizens of Ilidza voted for one MP in the Council of Municipalities, and the Serb candidate won absolutely. In Ilidza there were many more Serbs at the time than Muslims, so probably during the census there were people there who had come temporarily and registered there, Muslims, that is, and that's why there were more of them. But there were more Serbs there, actually, because the Serbs voted for the Serb MP and the Muslims voted for the Muslim candidate. But Ljubo Bosiljcic won. Before that Ilidza was considered a Serb municipality, but this census in 1991 was a highly objectionable one. Apparently many ballots were found that had not been used at all, and what was proclaimed was that in the entire municipality there were more Muslims than Serbs. That's it. That is why I'm saying that one has to understand by way of an analysis what the municipality of Ilidza is like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I wonder, could you be given the book of maps that we have. It's P527. And go to page 28. That is -- that's a map of -- it's a fairly simple one of Ilidza. Do you see that? And the legend, it shows built-up areas. It's -- well, yes. It shows built-up areas in a sort of yellow colour. In fact, the yellow-shaded areas go outside the boundaries of Ilidza, don't they, on that page?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this is Ilidza as far as I can see over here. I don't know what this is. No. Not this. Not this. This is not Ilidza. No. Sorry. Sorry. This is a mistake. Stup and all of this out here is Ilidza. And over here, that should be Novi Grad, because Nedzarici is in Novi Grad. So the border should be somewhere around here. All of this up here is Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think perhaps to clarify, Mr. Krajisnik, it's maybe not the most perfect map in the world. The boundary, and they are boundary lines aren't they the boundaries between those municipalities are those rather thin black lines on this map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is Ilidza, too, this up here, Kasindol and Ilidza -- no. Yes. Yes. You see this? This is a blue line, and all of this is Ilidza. Right. You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dogladi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek one clarification? Mr. Krajisnik said that Nedzarici is in Novo Sarajevo. It clearly, on this map, is in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you see the -- His Honour is pointing out that Nedzarici, it's actually just to the west of the black line which apparently marks the boundary between Ilidza and the adjoining municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the municipality that Nedzarici belongs to. Nedzarici does not belong to Ilidza. I don't know whether this is done very precisely, but Nedzarici is Novi Grad, not Novo Sarajevo. It was my municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I misspoke. Novi Grad. But on this map it appears to be -- it appears to be part of Ilidza. But perhaps that's not a vital matter, but just to be alert on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can you see this red point here? That's Nedzarici, and it's outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tend to disagree with you, Mr. Krajisnik. What I see is that the thin black lines are representing the boundaries of the municipalities, and I see that just before Nedzarici the thin black line turns relatively sharp east, and then soon after that turns north and west again and then continues up to where it comes to Bare. It might not be of major importance, but let's be alert on any possible mistakes on the exact position of the -- of the boundaries of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krajisnik, I've got to say as far as the positions on the map is concerned, with respect, I'm a hundred per cent with His Honour on where it is in relation to boundary, but you are saying, Mr. Krajisnik, are you, from your local knowledge, you're saying that you are absolutely sure that Nedzarici was in fact in the municipality of Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I agree with the Presiding Judge too. That's exactly what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, by the positioning on the map. But the second bit -- Mr. Krajisnik, forget for a moment about lines on maps. You lived there at the time, was Nedzarici in Novi Grad or was it in Ilidza? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to be clear: All my knowledge was that Nedzarici is in Novi Grad. However, the Presiding Judge is right here; the line looks as if it were on Ilidza. But all my knowledge is that Nedzarici was in Novi Grad, which was my municipality. Possibly the boundary was somewhere nearby. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, at these discussions or at this meeting that you had with the Ilidza leadership, was there any discussion about members of any ethnic group having to leave the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but before that everybody fled to their own side, if I can put it that way. If they could. Once the problem broke out, many Serbs remained out there in Sokolovic or Kolonija. In this area here. And probably some Muslims remained in Ilidza. But most people separated like wine and water. People fled from that war. I don't know whether any one of them said something like that, but I know that the policy was to find a political solution. I don't know whether anybody mentioned at that time that somebody was supposed to be expelled, thrown out. I'm sure that no one said any such thing. Quite simply, Muslims fled towards Hrasnica and Serbs towards Ilidza. That's what I remember. This is the area of Kotorac, I think, and Kasindol, and then you'd hear telephone conversations. Muslims were here, I don't know in which area -- that's it, I think. That's on the outskirts of Ilidza. The telephone conversations that we had the opportunity of hearing here, actually, but in the centre of Ilidza, no, absolutely not. And no one had instructions to do any such thing either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you just please make clear, when you said in that answer that Muslims fled towards Hrasnica, by reference to a map, if you need to, which -- which direction is that and where were they going?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the centre of Ilidza. This is Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On that map on page 28, Your Honours, it's almost right in the middle of the page, just to the bottom of the very southern-most yellow-shaded area, if Your Honours see that. There are two places; Lasica and Hrasnica. I've just found it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's where we're talking about, aren't we, Mr. Krajisnik? So you're saying that Muslims fled to Hrasnica which was itself in the municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Correct. It's difficult to orient oneself on this map but I'll try to explain. This is downtown Ilidza, the centre of Ilidza, and the demarcation line was around here. So if some Muslims had lived there, they ran away to this side. Those Serbs who managed, ran across to the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... anything else. Just show us the demarcation line again, please. I was myself looking at something else.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see this is the centre of Ilidza. From that centre, the demarcation line was a hundred metres away. All this green area here is Serb land. Protected areas. That's why they were painted green. So Muslims ran to Hrasnica, which was predominantly - maybe 90 per cent - Muslim. There are lots of Serbs here, like in Glogovina and Stojcevac, but Hrasnica was larger built-up area, a Muslim area, and the Muslims ran up and the demarcation line was maybe just a hundred metres away from the centre of Ilidza. This is Stojcevac. UN headquarters used to be there but it was turned over to the Muslims and then this became the boundary line all the way to the centre of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying the demarcation line was already there on the ground at the time that you were having this meeting with Mr. Prstojevic and his colleagues, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there -- it could be again that there was some ambiguity introduced into the question in the way you heard it. Was this question of fleeing of Muslims, broadly to the south as you've described it, and Serbs broadly towards the town of Ilidza, was that discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't rule out the possibility that we discussed it. However, it wasn't the main topic. I cannot say in the affirmative that we discussed the subject of fleeing. We talked about the war. Our people were on one side, their people were on the other side. We didn't know how many Serbs or Muslims were in Ilidza. There were both ethnic communities there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about any plans or prospective attempts to gain territory south of the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I now? At that meeting -- actually, whatever I now say about that meeting would be pure improvisation, but I'm trying to help. At that time, we didn't really know -- in fact, we knew whose ethnic area they were, but the war was beginning, and there must have been some local demands to liberate certain neighbourhoods from that or the other side, depending on who lived there. But at that meeting, lots of topics of all kinds were discussed. I forgot most of them. It wasn't a serious meeting, it was just talking, chatting, an exchange of information, but there was no serious briefing or preparation of plans, especially because this leadership of Ilidza didn't seem to think they needed to listen to anyone. They seemed intent on doing whatever suited them. And Mr. Prstojevic himself was known as a stubborn, self-willed person. He was a very conscientious worker, a hard worker, but he liked to do everything himself, on his own, and he wasn't easily put under control, nor did anyone try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said they seemed intent on doing whatever suited them. Did it appear -- was anything that they were apparently intending to do something of which you disapproved?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your questions sound very simple, but actually it's very hard to answer them. I can only say again that I have a certain experience that I can tell you about and that applied from that time. Every municipality, including the municipality of Ilidza, whenever they were able to deal with something themselves did not report anything or ask anybody for help. Only if they needed assistance did they inform somebody else about their problems. But if they had an affair to deal with, good or bad, and they were able to deal with it themselves, they did. I'm not going to say that the autonomy of municipalities was absolute, but it was great. The system that we had in Bosnia and Herzegovina fell apart, and new times began. Some new people appeared on the scene, and they dealt with problems as best they knew how. I only received people who needed some sort of help or intervention, but they never asked for advice. They never said, "Look, we are dealing with this or that. What do you think about it?" This leadership thought about themselves as mature, and indeed they were, and they dealt with most of their problems themselves. They were, among other things, a wealthy area, so they did not need assistance that much. They rarely addressed the government for help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when Mr. Kecmanovic gave evidence in this case he described meetings at which you, whoever else was present, at which you and he and Mr. Pejanovic were present. Was Mr. Kecmanovic correct in saying that there were, in the course of April and May, whenever precisely the meetings took place, that there were two meetings at which you and he and Mr. Pejanovic were present? Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were two different meetings at two different locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first meeting, without worrying for the moment, Mr. Krajisnik, about when exactly they were, at which location was the first meeting? Being as precise as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I described that meeting at Ilidza. As for the other meeting, I can show you the location that the three of us visited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the -- the Ilidza meeting, it was in a hotel, was it, Mr. Krajisnik? And if so, can you be specific?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which hotel, so we have that clear from you? Do you remember which hotel?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wrong about that. The hotel is called this is half Bosnia and half Serbia. There were two wings to it. One is called Bosna, and the other is called Serbia. He said that it was at the Terme Hotel, but it was not. It was at this other hotel, half of which was Bosnia, half was Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was another hotel across the road called Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to you, Mr. Kecmanovic got the hotel wrong. And then the second of the meetings that was attended by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just looking at the clock and having arrived at a hotel, should we not take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a good place and time to do it, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, have you placed the first of those meetings at the Srbija Hotel or Bitava [phoen] Hotel in Ilidza, what -- what do you recall as the subject of discussion between -- well, first of all -- I beg your pardon. There was Mr. Kecmanovic, Mr. Pejanovic, and you. Was anybody else present at the meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic. I don't know if anybody else was there, but the two of them certainly were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Yes, absolutely, throughout the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recall what was the topic or what were the topics of discussion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two delegations there that day. They had come to inform themselves and to be mediators between the warring parties, to help organise a meeting, contact, in order to find a solution that would stop the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, that -- my question is at the meeting, leaving aside the two delegations, at the meeting among you, Mr. Karadzic, Koljevic, Kecmanovic, and Mr. Pejanovic, what was the subject at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topic for that meeting -- in fact, the purpose of that meeting was that they had come to talk to us to hear what our position was so that we could find a solution that would stop the war, and they suggested that a meeting should be held. That indeed later happened. Al meeting where they would mediate with the other side so that the other side accepts to attend that meeting at a location to be agreed. Maybe there were other topics, but I remember only that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you inform them as to your position in relation to finding a solution that would stop the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether we actually said it to them, but the conversation focused on finding the relevant -- the competent people to meet with so that we can talk to the leadership in Sarajevo later to try to stop the war together with them. Goodwill was expressed to them. They wanted to be mediators so that we could meet and find a solution. I cannot be precise as to whether there were any proposals made. There may have been, but I don't want to speculate now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss the -- any proposal for the division of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to emphasise that Sarajevo was indeed the topic of discussion, but it was foremost in the minds of the three of us that we cannot agree to any option whereby Sarajevo would end up in their Muslim hands. We wanted to make a point that Serbs have as much of a right to Sarajevo as the Muslims do. It has become a rule of sorts to think of Zagreb as a Croat centre, Belgrade as the Serb centre, Sarajevo as the Muslim centre, but we thought we wanted to make a point that nobody has a right to isolate us out of Sarajevo. It was our intention to discuss a transformation of Sarajevo whereby we would have control over certain parts. The answer to your question is that as far as I remember, Sarajevo was discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any criticisms offered by Mr. Kecmanovic, Mr. Pejanovic as to the policy and position of you and your colleagues in the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not then. Their only wish was to get information and to mediate. They, too, advocated that the war should be stopped and a solution found. I am certain that there was no resistance on their part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question? Mr. Krajisnik, you said that it was your intention to discuss the transformation of it prior to that -- you said that you "could not agree to any option whereby Sarajevo would end up in their Muslim hands. We wanted to make a point that Serbs have as much of a right to Sarajevo as the Muslims do." Now, you earlier explained to us that as a temporary solution you would rather freeze the situation where, I would say the centre of the city was in Muslim hands, and quite a bit to the west whereas some areas around the old town were under Serbian control at that time. Would that be a situation which you would consider that Sarajevo would be in the Muslim hands, or would that at this time of this meeting be acceptable as a solution even if it were only a temporary solution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Stewart asked me, at least that's what I understood, what our policy on Sarajevo was in general, whereas you are asking me now what I talked about with Mr. Izetbegovic, along what lines. The point was to stop the war and then to talk about Sarajevo. And when I said that we had never accepted that anybody should isolate us out of Sarajevo so that we would have no rights, no control over there just because somebody things we have Belgrade and Sarajevo is a purely Muslim city, that's completely separate from these talks, because Sarajevo is also a Serb town. But throughout, we intended to talk about Sarajevo, that it should remain one town, whereas on the local level we have rights over certain parts. But if they create a town where everything is ruled from the centre, then there's no chance of that. Our point was to freeze things for a while so as to find a solution. We did not discuss a permanent solution with Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for purposes of what your policy was, would finally a settlement on the basis of the frozen situation have been acceptable to you, or did you say, "No, we were entitled to more of Sarajevo as we held at that time"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have documents about what we had said to Mr. Cutileiro as to what our proposal was.
