When we were talking about peace, we said that Sarajevo would have a small extra-territorial part where the state institutions would be located. Then there would be another part with mainly Muslim municipalities that would be under their control, would belong to them. Like here. That's a Muslim majority. And if we were to follow an ethnic principle, then the Serbs would get the periphery, because you cannot take any areas where the Muslims have a majority. If we were to discuss that. So we said that in this part here, since Bosnia was a state that we were going to accept, there should be an extra-territorial part state institutions would be located such as parliament, the government, et cetera. And as for the rest, we should see whether there are any neighbourhoods even in the urban area where the Serbs had a majority, like Pofalici. We were aware, nevertheless, that this is a Muslim-majority area, and we never disputed that. We didn't want to take that area away from them. However, we were not even looking for a permanent solution with Mr. Izetbegovic. We only discussed a temporary solution starting with ending the war. And that proposal exists somewhere in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So restructuring was needed for a final solution, and you would have to look in more detail at what exactly would be -- you mentioned Pofalici from -- Pofalici was at that time under Muslim control, but you considered it should be part of the Serbian part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just mentioned incidentally an ethnic unit. But let me try to assist you, Your Honour. We have shorthand notes from a session of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina where Mr. Silajdzic describes our conversation, our talks about Sarajevo, and he himself seems to be in favour of it. There was no suggestion of division, because that would have been impossible. How can you divide a town if you're not dividing a country? Transformation is something different. And it's quite another matter that the word "division" can be understood in different ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what you told us before. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And I appreciate this opportunity to clarify things, because it's important that they be clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you've said that they, and that's Mr. Kecmanovic and Mr. Pejanovic, they, too, advocated that the war should be stopped and a solution found. Did they have any ideas or suggestions of their own as to where that solution might be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I know what their opinion was from before the war. However, I don't remember any representations they made at that meeting. I don't think, actually, they suggested anything specific. They only wanted that meeting to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- did they offer any criticisms of your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think as far as that is concerned, how the war started in Sarajevo, Mr. Karadzic was rather indignant. He said we wouldn't leave Sarajevo like that. There was a fierce debate but no criticism. They thought that we were against the meeting, and they were happy when we accepted it. But it was quite the contrary. We wanted that meeting, too, because we wanted very much to find a solution. At least I don't remember any criticism, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there discussion of what was happening in the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I don't remember, but I'm almost certain that we didn't touch upon that topic. My answer is that I can't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you -- had you had any sort of meeting or discussion with Mr. Kecmanovic and Mr. Pejanovic before this particular meeting and quite recently?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already answered that I had two meetings. I think it was the second one, the one that wasn't held at Ilidza. It was held later. I'm certain it was held later. So I didn't have any meetings before the war, I'm sure, with the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you hadn't seen either Mr. Kecmanovic or Mr. Pejanovic the previous day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I think there was just that one meeting. I mean at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the later meeting, then, that was in Lukavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a bit further from Lukavica. Tilava, maybe, not really Tilava but somewhere here. It belongs to Lukavica but it's on the outskirts of Lukavica. It used to be a community club or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could say how much longer -- how long after the first meeting that you've described at the Hotel Srbija was this other meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was already at Pale at the time. I think I had been -- I think it was a month or maybe even two months later. The end of May, the end of June. Around that time, but I can't be precise. We could time it relative to their entry into the Presidency, but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in due course, then, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, did you at some time still in April but after the meeting that you've just described at Hotel Srbija and after the meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic have a further meeting with General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that somewhere around that time I had that meeting with General Kukanjac that I described attended by a group of people who discussed and presented their wishes to Mr. Kukanjac, who didn't take them very seriously. At least he just heard them out and didn't do anything about it. I think it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was whether there was then a further meeting with -- with Mr. Kukanjac in the course of April.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any other meetings with Mr. Kukanjac apart from that one, although it's possible that I attended one more, but I don't remember any others. There was somebody there with Mr. Kukanjac, but I can't remember who. Excuse me. When I was talking about the Terme Hotel, the hotel Bosna and Srbija is very close to Hotel Terme, and that's probably why the error occurred. Bosna and Srbija are in one and the same building. Herzegovina is just across the road near a park, and Terme is just around a hundred metres away. I know we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in April, 1992, do you -- did you -- well, do you remember the first occasion in April, 1992, when you attended any sort of formal meeting in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would that meeting -- what was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Zabrdje, and my colleagues from Sarajevo, my former work colleagues at the company where I used to work, informed me that one of them was arrested, a Croat, and they asked me if I could get him released. Another call came from the Muslim side. I'm not quite sure, but I'm almost sure that it was Mr. Muhamed Filipovic who called. He said that some of his family had been arrested somewhere, and they asked me if I could help somehow. All I could do was get into a car and go to Pale. I thought I could find someone and see if there was anything I could do. I don't remember to whom I talked at that time. All I know is that the family of Mr. Cengic had -- was released, and that former work colleague of mine, Marinko Musa, was also released. That's what I managed to do on that day. Later on, I saw in the papers that it was on the 15th of April, and I attended a meeting that was called meeting of the National Security Council of the government, but actually all sorts of people were there discussing all sorts of things. And that was my first trip to Pale, after which I went back to Zabrdje which I spent several days, and then I went to Pale for good. That's the first meeting I remember where I participated in the discussion. Everybody who was there participated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like you to be given then, please, the minutes of -- it's called the minutes of the joint meeting of the National Security Council and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on 15th of April, 1992. It's P64 [Realtime transcript read in error "P65"], binder 22, tab 618.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the ERN number that I have is 01245291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, on the transcript it appears P65. I heard you saying P64. And on your list it appears as P64A.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have said -- I've made this mistake. It should be P64 A, Your Honour's quite right. 64A, binder 22, tab 618. It's also in P65, binder 11, tab 120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is the -- they are minutes of the meeting that you were just referring to, are they, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading these minutes, I understood that it was actually those minutes. However, had you asked me whether it was on the 15th, I could not have said had this document not been produced. I attended a meeting, and some of these topics here were ones that I was familiar with, but then I have to be quite honest. I'm not familiar with others. For example, Decision on the Establishment of the SRNA Serbian News Agency. It was established before I came to Pale, although, one can always allow for the possibility of a certain mix-up in one's head, but I certainly attended a meeting in April, and it's probably this date because it says here that I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this was, was it, the first meeting of this type that you attended in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here, and I can confirm that that is probably the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this point do you remember whether you were living in Pale or whether you went home after this meeting to Zabrdje?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not live in Pale. I went home to Zabrdje. Perhaps I just spent the night there and returned the next day, but I came particularly on account of this task and then I went home to Zabrdje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The item 1 -- you see who is present. I'm not going to go right through the list, but you are among them and the -- Dr. Radovan Karadzic, the president of the National Security Council chaired the meeting and the agenda that was adopted was, first, a manner of work in an emergency/war situation. The item 1: "It was concluded that meetings of the National Security Council and the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are to be held every day depending on the circumstances, but in principle in the Kikinda building in Pale." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you were a member of the national security council and we see subsequently a series of joint meetings. Were there during April and early May, 1992, separate meetings of either the National Security Council or the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was no legal body called the National Security Council. I can explain why I'm saying that. In response to your question, a special meeting was not held as far as I can remember of the government and this sort of council for national security. This is the way it was: Whoever happened to be there attended that meeting. Well, not exactly whoever happened to be there, but from among these high officials. That was the meeting that was called this in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The conclusion that meetings of National Security Council and the government were to be held every day depending on the circumstances and then the next item said, "Work will begin at 9.00, 0990 hours in the morning on a priority basis with a Council meeting and the development of a daily plan of operation." Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I'm talking about later when I came there. People lived in Kikinda, in the rooms there. And then when you'd get up in the morning, then you'd have a meeting and you'd discuss things. It's not that people came from somewhere for that. They were there. So there's a room where people spent time sort of like in a living-room, and then people sleep in other rooms. So the conclusion was that they should meet up every morning at 9.00 in order to have a discussion and to have a meeting held that way. It wasn't that way all the time, because somebody could be away on a trip. The organisation was rather poor. Mr. Djeric, in particular, and I, too, complained about the inefficiency of these meetings. Some people would sleep in late. Others would get up earlier. Somebody had left. Somebody was not staying in that building but in another building, and so on and so forth. So is wasn't regular but it was supposed to be regular. Morning consultations during coffee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And item 2, I just mention and don't dwell on it. The prime minister was authorised Mr. Djeric, wasn't it authorised to consult persons needed to fill the government posts. Then item 3, decision and conclusions "Reviewing the security situation in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was assessed that the conditions had been met to propose that the Presidency of the Republic declare a state of imminent threat of war." Did the meeting receive any reports for reaching that decision or conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such conclusions, but they weren't even needed. Quite simply, it was clear to everyone that this was a war and that it wasn't the pre-war time any longer. It's not that there was some information that was written and then presented. I don't recall any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it's over the page in the English, but it's the next paragraph. "It was also proposed that the Presidency adopt measures for the removal of the causes of the situation that has emerged." Was that just saying that the Presidency should try to stop the war, or was it saying something other than that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Presidency could not stop the war. When this was being discussed, that is to say this National Security Council, on the 24th of March and on the 27th of March, 1992, it was envisaged that the council as an advisory body, once it is constituted, should present proposals to the authorities, primarily to the Assembly and the Presidency. They were supposed to give advice. And what was suggested here was to introduce a state of imminent threat of war, which was done formally later as well. So how is a crisis announced? A situation where there is an imminent threat of war is proclaim, and then work is done on the solution of that crisis. According to the constitution, it should be the government making that kind of proposal. However, the discussion here indicates that it was the council that had proposed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are a number of decisions and conclusions adopted. You referred a few minutes ago to the formation of the Serbian news agency SRNA. Did you subsequently have any role yourself in the formation of such an agency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I arrived in Pale, I heard -- well, how shall I put this? - that there was this agency that was nominated or, rather, that was called SRNA. Mr. Karadzic named the agency SRNA. SRNA means the Serb radio -- oh, I'm sorry. Just a moment, please. Now, what is this abbreviation? The Serb radio news agency, SRNA. And that is why it was called SRNA. As for both, I did not know when these things happened, but I was informed about it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there was a decision on the appointment of the acting commander of the TO, the Territorial Defence, and the chief of staff of the -- of the TO. Do you recall who were appointed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall this decision, but I saw a decision that was signed by Mr. Djeric. Some Lukic had been appointed, Vidoje Lukic, whatever his name was, and he signed that decision for him. However, truth to tell, that man had no powers whatsoever. He was not in command. He did not carry out this function because he was completely cut off. So this was only very formal and very brief. I saw him once next to a room, but he really didn't have any authority and he was not really in office, but I was not informed about when this had been done. In fact, it was the government that -- actually, I have to say something. I assume that this consultative meeting was held and then somebody later on wrote these minutes and they put into these minutes things that had done previously too. That is my assumption. I mean, I know that some things were discussed, and then others happened before that but are in these minutes. So that is my explanation for that. I heard that these two things happened, but it wasn't that they were discussed at that meeting when I was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, as you say, Mr. Vidoje Lukic did not have powers and he didn't carry out this function, did somebody else then carry out those functions in practice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the Yugoslav People's Army was in existence. I remember the attack on Kupres. We were sitting there and we said, "Well, wait a minute. You're the commander. Are you going to do something about it?" They were simply walking around like we were. Nobody commanded these units. Until our army was established, all of this was under the JNA. At local level, whoever had this Territorial Defence simply had to do whatever they could. That was my impression. There were these telephone conversations seeking information and so on, but those were not orders, and no one could have issued orders. It was all dissipated. Every village had its own command, its own guard, and the Yugoslav People's Army was separate from that. So even that which existed relied upon the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Mladic at the time, Mr. Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, before he came to Sarajevo, to Lukavica, was commander of the Knin Corps. That is to say that he was in the Republic of the Serb Krajina before the Vance Plan. When Mr. Kukanjac was replaced, for a brief period of time he took his place, and he became commander of the 2nd Military District. For a brief period of time, until our army was establish. This did not go on for a long time, but I cannot say how long it went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at the time of this meeting, 15th of April, can you say where Mr. Mladic was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no idea whatsoever as to where he was. I assume that he was at that first place where he worked. He was not in Sarajevo. He was not with us. I think Mr. Kukanjac was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: "Every village had its own guard, its own command, and the Yugoslav People's Army was separated from that." [Interpretation] I would like to put a question to you. Had you did you know this at the time? What information did you have about what was going on in the field? You're telling us this, so did you learn this afterwards or at the time of the meeting of the National Security Council? Were you informed? Who informed you? And did you know what was happening on the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 15th of April, the only regular armed force is the Yugoslav People's Army. Before that, the members of the Presidency reached a decision, I think, to mobilise the Territorial Defence like the Muslim Territorial Defence, following that example. That is to say if there are people who hadn't been mobilised, they should be order. If you remember, on the 27th of March when Karadzic said, "Come on, make some units that would defend their own villages only." I'm just saying if you're already mobilising the Territorial Defence regardless of whether this is happening in actual fact or not, you have to have some kind of commander. So when this commander was appointed, I told you what kind of powers he had, none whatsoever because he didn't have any communication. I assume -- no, I don't assume. I'm sure that every settlement, every village, as soon as some kind of line of separation was established, had its own forces. There were some forces of these villages that protected the area if there was a line. They were protecting their own area. Now, what was the information I had. Like Ilidza, like my home Zabrdje, everybody defended their own ethnic areas. We can call this the armed people, the Territorial Defence, whatever, but this did exist. So you didn't really have to be very smart or to have lots of information to know that -- well, you know, that you know that there is some kind of separation line where there are Serbs on one side and Muslims on the other side, or, let's say, Croats on the other say and so on. I am talking about something -- well, if you were to ask me now on the basis of what did I know all of this, I would really have to try to remember where I heard this but that's the answer will the way it was. That's exactly the way it was. We had these armed people there defending their own villages, and we saw that from the documents. Now, this man was supposed to be their command, but he did not command them because he could not. The armed people relied upon the Yugoslav People's Army, and that is why we established our own army later, because the JNA was supposed to go to Serbia. That would be it, if I managed to give you an explanation. That existed. I saw that in my very own village, in Ilidza, and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the meetings which have been mentioned in your evidence today with General Kukanjac, up to this point, 15th of April when this meeting was held, since the start of the war had you had any direct contact yourself with any military commanders anywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the 15th or later? I beg your pardon. Up to the 15th of April or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up could this point, Mr. Krajisnik, since the start of the war. In this relatively short period.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from this meeting with Mr. Kukanjac you mean. Your excluding that meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except on the local level. Except on local level. There was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, since I was president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One day he came to see me. To this day I don't know what his name is. He brought me some kind of radio transmitter so that I could communicate. This went on for about two days or whatever, not more than that. But there were no other contacts that I had. I was not in contact with anyone else. Mr. Kukanjac stayed in Sarajevo, and he was in contact through JuTel and others, but I did not have any communication with him because I was at a different locality. I don't remember having any meetings. As for all the persons mentioned here, I did not have any contact with them. Through the mentioned process, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, have you dealt with the document or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I haven't finished with it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- as far as you were aware, did General Mladic have any input to the discussions, decisions, information of this group that met on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I mean, I didn't even know -- well, it wasn't that I didn't even know, but I didn't think about him ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there are a number of conclusions, then, under the heading "The following was also concluded." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then a number of items are set out, and in particular, going about eight lines down: "To notify," do you see that, "To notify all the political leaderships of the Serbian autonomous districts and the state leader ships of the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro that cooperate and other contacts between them are to be conducted through the official organs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." As far as you were concerned, Mr. Krajisnik, was that a -- was that a formal step or was it a step with significant practical implications?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this was translated, but what it says here is to send a request -- I don't know where you find this. Where is that written? Oh, yes, I see. I see. "An appeal to the Yugoslav and international public as well as the United Nations." Is that it? No. I beg your pardon. Sorry. I found it. I found it. Well, I cannot remember all the details now, but I know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? Every municipality, every autonomous region went out looking for assistance on their own autonomously. They contacted the authorities in Serbia and so on and so forth. No one gave the leadership of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina any serious role. And now this, to make an appeal, that there was some kind of leadership. It had even been proclaimed that they had fled somewhere and that it did not exist. When I said at that there was no National Security Council, Mr. Karadzic was supposed to speak up as the top person there, but we didn't want to say that he was the president of the party, because then it would turn out that it was some kind of war waged by the SDS. So what was said then, that it should be the government, which is not there and was not complete. And there should be the National Security Council, because, the party used to have a document entitled "National Security Council." So he was the only president of that council. And this council for national security had never been constituted, actually. We were supposed to pretend that there is some kind of joint authority and that there are not 100 municipalities, but then there's some kind of authority that's speaking up and saying, "Wait a minute. We're here." And there should be contact. It should go through us not every autonomous region behaving like state in its own right. After all, necessity compelled them to do that, but on the other hand they were doing it themselves too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it says: "Presidency member Professor Biljana Plavsic is authorised to represent the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in contacts with the United Nations regarding the newly emerged situation." Did that happen? Did she take over that role in practice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic was in Sarajevo at the time, in her own apartment. This was made public at this meeting, and then she was in contact with the UN, and then information was provided to the effect that what Mrs. Plavsic was doing, namely that she was in contact with them, that this body authorised her to have contact with the UN. This was also by way of a declaration to hear that she was authorised and behalf of the Serb republic, because before that the two of them had resigned from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mrs. Plavsic liaise with or consult you in relation to this work of hers with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way, she was isolated in her apartment. And we were worried about her safety. And this Mr. Doyle did quite a bit for her not to be left at the mercy of these gangs that ruled Sarajevo at the time. So if there were any contacts, there were one or two, but not in relation to this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the next item, Professor Koljevic was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for one clarification. You said Mrs. Plavsic was in her apartment in Sarajevo. How long did she stay there? It may have been already in evidence but then I've forgotten about it. When did she come to Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a paper here. If you remember when a protected witness testified, it was made public that on the 20th of April she was taken prisoner in Sarajevo, and that on the 22nd she went out to Pale. That is what the SRNA news says. I know what I read there. I beg your pardon. She did not stay in Pale straight away. She went back and then she travelled to Zvornik, Foca, and so on, but on that day she went to Pale from Sarajevo. As a matter of fact, I think that she actually returned to Sarajevo again. I'm not sure. But Mrs. Plavsic was not at our Assembly in Banja Luka on the 12th of May. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I wanted to know, as a matter of fact, is how long that situation of isolation in Sarajevo in her apartment lasted. That's clear now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said please proceed, but it's 7.00. Mr. Krajisnik, we'll adjourn for the day. I instruct you again, you could even say it yourself, not to speak to anybody about your testimony you either already given or still to be given. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past two, and as I announced there is a fair chance we might finish early tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, when might we know that fair chance has come about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is something that cannot be planned. It could be that we know only at 3.00, 4.00, 9.00 in the morning. It's totally unpredictable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, that's helpful, that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we adjourn until tomorrow, same courtroom, quarter past two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 12th day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
